title: The penalty kick
question: A footballer takes a powerful penalty. Estimate the average force of the boot on the ball.
think: The mass of a football
How fast it leaves the boot
How long the boot touches the ball
steps: Mass of a football: about 0.4 kg. Speed after the kick: about 25 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Contact time: about 0.01 s.
Average force = rate of change of momentum: $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} \approx \dfrac{0.4 \times 25}{0.01} \approx 1000$ N.
note: That's about the weight of a 100 kg person, on a ball that weighs about 4 N. The contact time is the least certain value here, and a shorter contact means a larger force.

title: Burning off the chocolate
question: A chocolate bar's wrapper says that it provides about 1000 kJ. Estimate how many flights of stairs you would have to climb to use up that energy.
think: Your mass
The height of one flight of stairs
What fraction of the energy from food your muscles turn into useful work
steps: Useful work per flight: $mg\Delta h \approx 60 \times 9.8 \times 3 \approx 1800$ J.
Muscles are only about 25% efficient, so the useful work available from the bar is about $0.25 \times 1.0 \times 10^{6} = 2.5 \times 10^{5}$ J.
Number of flights $\approx \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{5}}{1800} \approx 140$.
note: If you left out the efficiency you got about 550 flights, and that is still within a factor of 10. Being explicit about efficiency is what makes the estimate better.

title: The air in your classroom
question: Estimate the mass of the air in your classroom.
think: The length, width and height of the room
The density of air
steps: Volume of a typical classroom: about $9 \times 7 \times 3 \approx 190$ $\text{m}^3$.
Density of air: about 1.2 $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.
Mass $= \rho V \approx 1.2 \times 190 \approx 230$ kg.
note: About the mass of three or four adult students. Air feels like nothing because we are surrounded by it, but it certainly has mass. Your own room's measurements will give a slightly different answer.

title: Molecules in a glass of water
question: Estimate the number of water molecules in an ordinary glass of water.
think: The mass of water in a glass
The molar mass of water
The Avogadro constant
steps: A glass holds about 250 g of water. The molar mass of water is about 18 $\text{g mol}^{-1}$, so that's $250 \div 18 \approx 14$ mol.
Number of molecules $\approx 14 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \approx 8 \times 10^{24}$.
note: That's more than the number of stars in the observable universe, which most estimates put at between about $10^{22}$ and $10^{24}$.

title: Electrons through a phone
question: Estimate how many electrons pass through a phone's charging cable during one full charge.
think: A typical battery capacity (look for mAh on a phone's specification)
How to turn mAh into coulombs
The charge on one electron
steps: A typical phone battery holds about 4000 mAh: a current of 4 A for 1 hour.
Charge $= It = 4 \times 3600 \approx 14\,000$ C.
Number of electrons $= \dfrac{14\,000}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 9 \times 10^{22}$.
note: An enormous number, but remember that charge isn't used up: these electrons flow round the circuit. What the charger supplies is energy. (The cable's voltage differs a little from the battery's, so the real number is a bit lower, but it's the same order of magnitude.)

title: Light across a hair
question: Estimate how many wavelengths of red light would fit across the width of one human hair.
think: The width of a hair
The wavelength of red light
steps: A hair is about 70 µm wide, which is $7 \times 10^{-5}$ m.
Red light has a wavelength of about 650 nm, which is $6.5 \times 10^{-7}$ m.
Number of wavelengths $\approx \dfrac{7 \times 10^{-5}}{6.5 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 110$.
note: A hair is only about a hundred wavelengths wide, narrow enough for a laser beam to spread out noticeably around it. That's why a hair gives a clear diffraction pattern on a screen a metre or two away.

title: The pull between two people
question: Two students stand about 1 m apart. Estimate the gravitational force between them.
think: The mass of each student
Which equation applies, and which constant it needs
steps: Take each mass as about 70 kg, and treat the students as point masses 1 m apart. This is a rough model for objects of this size.
$F = G\dfrac{m_1 m_2}{r^2} \approx 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times \dfrac{70 \times 70}{1^2} \approx 3 \times 10^{-7}$ N.
note: About the weight of a few grains of fine sand. We notice gravity only when one of the masses is as large as a planet.

title: Riding the Earth
question: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach us. Use this to estimate how fast the Earth is moving around the Sun.
think: How far light travels in about 8 minutes
The distance the Earth travels in one orbit
The number of seconds in a year
steps: Distance to the Sun: $r \approx 3.0 \times 10^{8} \times 500 \approx 1.5 \times 10^{11}$ m (8 minutes 20 seconds is 500 s).
One year is about $3.2 \times 10^{7}$ s.
Speed $= \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} \approx \dfrac{2\pi \times 1.5 \times 10^{11}}{3.2 \times 10^{7}} \approx 3 \times 10^{4}$ $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
note: About 30 km every second, and none of us can feel it. The Earth's centripetal acceleration is tiny (about $6 \times 10^{-3}$ $\text{m s}^{-2}$), and uniform motion can't be felt anyway.

title: A day at the power station
question: A large nuclear power station delivers about 1 GW of electrical power. Estimate the mass that is converted to energy in its reactor in one day.
think: The efficiency of a power station
The number of seconds in a day
How mass and energy are related
steps: If the station is about one-third efficient, the reactor releases about 3 GW.
Energy in a day: $E = Pt \approx 3 \times 10^{9} \times 8.6 \times 10^{4} \approx 2.6 \times 10^{14}$ J.
Mass: $m = \dfrac{E}{c^2} \approx \dfrac{2.6 \times 10^{14}}{(3.0 \times 10^{8})^2} \approx 3 \times 10^{-3}$ kg.
note: About 3 grams, roughly the mass of a small coin, converted in a whole day while supplying a large city. This isn't the mass of fuel used, which is far greater; it's only the decrease in the total mass of the nuclei and neutrons, which appears as the energy released.

title: How long will the Sun last?
question: The Sun has a mass of about $2 \times 10^{30}$ kg and a luminosity of about $3.8 \times 10^{26}$ W. Fusing hydrogen into helium converts about 0.7% of the hydrogen's mass into energy. Only the hot core, about a tenth of the Sun's mass, is available for fusion. Estimate how long the Sun can keep shining, in years.
think: The mass available for fusion
The energy released when mass is converted ($E = mc^2$)
The number of seconds in a year
steps: The core holds about 10% of the Sun's mass: about $2 \times 10^{29}$ kg.
Mass converted to energy: $0.007 \times 2 \times 10^{29} = 1.4 \times 10^{27}$ kg, so $E = mc^2 \approx 1.3 \times 10^{44}$ J.
Time $= \dfrac{E}{L} \approx \dfrac{1.3 \times 10^{44}}{3.8 \times 10^{26}} \approx 3 \times 10^{17}$ s, which is about $1 \times 10^{10}$ years.
note: About ten billion years, and the Sun is roughly halfway through. If you assumed that all of the Sun's mass could fuse, you'd be about ten times too high: only the core is hot enough for fusion.
